# The Warehouse Programme — Notes Written Before We Pick a Vendor

*Deliberately drafted before the demo trip. Anything written after you've stood inside a working goods-to-person cell is not analysis, it's a souvenir.*

---

## The number that decides most of this, and it isn't the payback

Thirty-five per cent picker turnover reads as a problem in the brief. I'd read it as the budget for the entire workforce transition, and I'd read it before I read anything the vendors sent.

Round arithmetic: if the network runs on the order of a thousand pick-side bodies, we are losing something like three hundred and fifty people a year, and have been, quietly, for years. Nobody notices because we backfill on Monday. That means the total headcount reduction any automation programme could plausibly want — call it a quarter to a third of pick labour over five years — is already walking out of the door on its own, roughly three times over, without a single difficult conversation.

Which reframes the whole exercise. We are not deciding whether to reduce a workforce. We are deciding **how much of the reduction we allow attrition to do for us, and that is purely a function of how early we start and how much slower than the vendors we are willing to go.** Every quarter we delay converts a resignation we'd have got for free into a redundancy we have to pay for, explain, and read about.

There is a second-order effect that I think settles the strategy. Attrition is concentrated almost entirely in the under-eighteen-months cohort. The tenured don't leave. So a shrink-by-not-backfilling policy automatically preserves precisely the cohort we most want to keep and most owe something to — the people who know how the site actually runs — and thins the cohort that is generating most of the error rate anyway. The humane path and the cheap path are, unusually, the same path. They only stay the same path if we begin now and refuse to be hurried later.

I'd take one decision off the table immediately and permanently: **no site converts faster than its own attrition curve allows.** That's the governing constraint. Capital availability, vendor schedules and payback models are all subordinate to it. If that costs us eight months of savings, we've bought them back in the cost of not being the next competitor on the news.

---

## What the vendors' three-year payback is actually made of

I'd want the payback decomposed before anyone quotes it again in a meeting, because I suspect a third of it is ours already and another third is a forecast dressed as a saving.

Three buckets:

**Labour hours removed.** Real, and probably understated, because our own baseline is almost certainly wrong in our favour — I doubt we're fully loading turnover. Recruiting, agency premium, the eight-week ramp, the overtime that covers the gap, the supervisor time spent training the same job for the ninth time. The true cost of a picker is likely 1.4–1.6× the wage line. Which cuts both ways, and that's the interesting part: a properly loaded baseline makes automation look better *and* makes simply fixing retention look better. The comparison is what we're actually deciding, and we currently can't make it.

**Errors eliminated.** Here I'd push hard. What fraction of our error rate is a robotics problem, and what fraction is a *"forty per cent of my pickers have been here under six months"* problem, compounded by slotting nobody's touched in four years and a label design that puts two similar SKUs three inches apart? The vendors are being paid to attribute all of it to the absence of their machine. I'd want that tested, cheaply, in about ninety days: one site, no capital, fix slotting on the fast-movers, redesign the labels, put a retention bonus and a proper buddy system on new hires, and measure. If errors fall meaningfully, we've just discovered that part of the promised return doesn't require the machine — and we've also established the only honest baseline against which the machine can later be judged.

I'd expect that pilot to be unpopular internally, because it delays the exciting thing. That's roughly what I'd use it for.

**Throughput headroom.** Real but conditional on volume growth we don't control. I'd score it at zero in the business case and treat it as upside. Capital that only pays back if the forecast lands is a bet on the forecast, not on the technology.

---

## A decision that comes before any site decision: how many warehouses do we want?

Automating a site is a ten-to-fifteen-year commitment to that site's existence at roughly that site's shape. Fixed automation is poured, not placed.

So before we sequence anything, I'd settle the network map — leases, growth by region, drive-time coverage, what a four-site or six-site network would look like. Not because I want to close anything, but because the worst available outcome is spending eight figures automating a building we'd have exited in 2029, and the second-worst is discovering the network logic *after* the town site has been converted and can no longer be discussed honestly.

I'd get that settled quietly and early, by a small group, and I'd be careful about the reverse failure: the network review becoming a stealth closure programme with a spreadsheet for a face. If the answer is five sites, we say five sites and we mean it for a decade.

---

## Degree: automate the head of the curve, leave the tail to people

The vendors will present a spectrum from voice-directed picking to lights-out. I'd sit deliberately, and probably permanently, in the middle, on two bets.

**Bet one: the Pareto line is the design.** Twenty per cent of SKUs will be seventy per cent of picks. Automate that head — goods-to-person for the fast-movers, put-walls and pick-to-light for the error-dense multi-line orders, print-and-apply, sortation, and dockside palletising because it's where the backs go. Leave the long tail — the awkward, the slow, the seasonal, the one-off — manual, on purpose, forever. The last thirty per cent of automation coverage costs more than the first seventy and eliminates the flexibility that lets a site absorb a surprise. It also happens to preserve a real, skilled, non-token category of human work, which we will need for reasons I'll come to.

**Bet two: modular over monolithic, even at a worse headline payback.** Mobile robots and add-a-cell architectures let us buy capacity in units of ten thousand rather than units of ten million, stop between increments, redeploy hardware to another site if a region disappoints, and — critically — keep running manually while we install. A shuttle ASRS is a better machine and a worse decision at our stage of knowledge. I'd accept a payback of four years for the option to stop at any point over three years for a bet we can't unwind.

One unglamorous prerequisite the vendors will wave past: **automation amplifies bad master data.** Dimensions, weights, cube, images, on 95%+ of active SKUs, verified not inherited. If we don't have that, no fixed-automation decision should be signed, because the machine will find every gap at peak, in November. I'd fund a data and slotting cleanup as phase zero and I'd let it be boring.

---

## Sequence — chosen for what each site teaches, not for which pays back fastest

The vendors will want to start where the contract is biggest. That is the largest site, which is the town, which is the one place a mistake is unrecoverable. I'd invert it.

**Site 1 — the learning site.** Mid-size, mid-complexity, nearest our engineering people, healthiest local labour market. The one we are permitted to get wrong. Full instrumented conversion of the fast-mover head, two vendors given adjacent scope if we can arrange it. Twelve to fifteen months. Its output is not savings; it's a truthful cost-per-line curve, a fault log, and an installation playbook written by people who now have scars.

**Site 2 — the tight labour market.** Wherever we can't fill the roles anyway, where we're running on agency temps at a premium and still short. Automation there displaces vacancies, not people. Lowest human cost in the network, highest immediate relief, and it lets us claim an early win that nobody has to be laid off for. Runs partly in parallel with Site 1 once the playbook exists.

**Site 3 — the account-damage site.** Wherever the errors are hurting the named customers. The case here is quality, not labour, and I'd say so publicly and internally, because it's true and because it sets the programme's story as *"we stopped shipping the wrong thing"* rather than *"we replaced people."*

**Site 4 — the flex site.** The oldest, smallest, most awkward building. Candidate for light automation only — pick-to-light, voice, better slotting — and for a deliberate role as the network's long-tail and surge capacity. Every automated network needs a manual shock absorber. Naming one on purpose is cheaper than discovering you needed one.

**Site 5 — the town.** Last to convert. First to be told. More on this below.

Rough arc: phase zero and the no-capital error pilot in the first two quarters; Site 1 through the following year and a bit; Sites 2 and 3 across years two and three; Site 4's light touch whenever it's convenient; the town beginning year three at the earliest, and only if Sites 1–3 have actually delivered. Anyone who wants those dates tighter is welcome to explain which part of the attrition constraint they'd like to break.

---

## The town

Largest warehouse, principal employer, and therefore the site where the difference between a considered programme and a competent-looking one becomes a news story with a photograph of a car park.

What I'd commit to, early, in writing, before anyone asks:

The site converts last, and it converts through attrition only. No involuntary separation of anyone with five or more years' service, for the life of the programme, network-wide — and at that site, no involuntary separation at all. If that constraint makes the site's own business case marginal, then the site's business case is that it stays open, which is a perfectly respectable thing for a business case to be.

The site becomes the network's **technical hub** rather than its most automated one: maintenance and reliability training, the spares depot, the crew that installs and supports the other four. Those are better jobs than the ones being displaced and they are geographically sticky. I'd fund a two-year technician apprenticeship with the local community college and I'd fill it from the existing crew by application, starting *before* the first robot ships. Not after. The sequencing there is the entire difference between retraining and outplacement with a nicer name.

And I'd point new volume — new customers, new categories, value-added services, returns processing, kitting — at that building preferentially. Reducing headcount by holding it flat while the site does more is invisible, gradual, and doesn't require anybody to be brave.

One thing I'd handle myself rather than delegate: the town's version of this story gets told first by us, to the mayor and the local paper, in person, before there is anything dramatic to report. A commitment made when nothing is happening is credible. The identical commitment made in week one of a conversion is a denial.

---

## People, in order of operations

**Stop backfilling before you start converting.** Site by site, twelve to eighteen months ahead of its own conversion date. It is the single highest-leverage act in the programme and it costs nothing but foresight. It does raise overtime and agency spend in the interim — I'd accept that line rising and I'd defend it in the review, because it is literally the price of not making people redundant.

**Watch for adverse selection, which is the actual workforce risk.** The moment a workforce senses automation, the first people to leave are the ones with options — the best, the most mobile, the ones we were counting on to run the new cells. Blanket retention bonuses waste money on people who weren't going anywhere. I'd target retention money narrowly and unapologetically: the tenured, the accurate, the ones supervisors would fight to keep. And I'd track high-performer attrition as a primary programme metric, not an HR footnote. If it moves, we've communicated badly, whatever the survey says.

**Say the guarantee, never the number.** No public headcount target, ever. Instead a promise we can actually keep: *every role affected is met with a funded alternative* — a role at this site, a role elsewhere with relocation paid properly rather than technically, retraining with a wage bridge for the gap, or an exit package we'd be comfortable seeing quoted. I'd budget that at ten to fifteen per cent of programme capital as a line item with its own name, approved once, at the start, so it can't be trimm
